title: Design a Batched LLM Inference Service
prompt:
Design a batched LLM inference service backed by a GPU fleet. The service should improve throughput while keeping latency predictable for client workloads ranging from a single input to a list of 100 inputs.

The core exercise uses a fixed-batch contract: a request becomes a durable job, the scheduler forms fixed batches, and GPU workers execute them. Do not use continuous batching or traffic rate limiting as the primary answer. State the SLOs and product assumptions you need before choosing the batch size and wait window.

Cover:

- API semantics for submission, idempotency, cancellation, status, and result retrieval.
- The durable write path, queueing model, fixed-batch scheduler, GPU-aware dispatch, and worker lifecycle.
- The correct latency objective for an asynchronous batch job versus a streaming interactive variant: queue time, end-to-end completion, time to first token (TTFT), and time per output token (TPOT, also called inter-token latency or ITL).
- How batch size and wait time trade off throughput, cost, queue delay, p95/p99 latency, fairness, model placement, and GPU memory.
- How two independent requests that share a system prompt, document, or conversation prefix can reuse prefix KV blocks; distinguish this from the ordinary request-private autoregressive decode KV cache.
- Cache-aware routing, cache eviction, multi-tenant isolation, partial failures, retries, scaling the GPU fleet, observability, and capacity signals.
- How you would review a flawed design document for missing assumptions, queue/scheduler mismatch, unsafe retry behavior, or a latency dashboard that hides cache misses.

This is a practice reconstruction of a recurring Anthropic ML-systems design signal from the Opportunity 2026 question bank. It preserves the reported batch-inference and review-mode themes, but is not presented as a verbatim interview script or a confirmed interviewer rubric.

response.placeholder: State the workload and SLOs first. Separate batch completion metrics from streaming TTFT and TPOT, then explain fixed batching, prefix-cache routing, failure handling, and trade-offs.
response.reference_answer:
## 1. Start by separating the product contracts

First ask whether this is an asynchronous batch job, a streaming interactive API, or both. For a pure asynchronous job, the customer-facing objectives are accepted-write latency, p95/p99 time to completion, cost per generated token, and job success rate. TTFT is not a user-visible objective if the user only polls for a completed result.

For a streaming variant, TTFT is the elapsed time until the first emitted token. TPOT, often reported as inter-token latency or ITL, is the gap between later output tokens. End-to-end latency measures completion. I would report p50, p95, and p99 separately by input length, requested output length, model, priority class, and prefix-cache hit or miss. A useful decomposition is TTFT = queue wait + scheduling + uncached prefill + first decode step + transport.

## 2. API and durable state

POST /v1/batches accepts a model version, inputs, generation parameters, a client-provided idempotency key, and an optional service class. It returns a batch_id only after the job and its items are durably recorded. GET /v1/batches/{id} returns Accepted, Queued, Leased, Running, Succeeded, Failed, or Cancelled plus per-item state and result locations. A streaming endpoint, if required, uses the same durable request ID and emits tokens after it enters Running.

The idempotency key maps to the durable job record, so a timeout retry returns the original batch_id rather than duplicating GPU work. Individual item IDs let a retry execute only unfinished items after a partial worker failure.

## 3. Fixed-batch baseline

An API tier validates the request, writes the job and items to durable storage, and appends a queue record through the same transaction or an outbox. Queues are partitioned by compatible execution shape: model version, hardware class, adapter, and coarse input/output-length bucket. The scheduler chooses eligible work fairly across service classes, waits at most W milliseconds, and dispatches a fixed batch when it reaches B compatible items or W expires.

B and W are explicit control knobs. Larger B and longer W usually improve GPU occupancy and tokens per dollar, but increase queue wait and p95 latency. A fixed-batch job remains fixed after dispatch; continuous batching is an extension to discuss only after solving the stated baseline.

## 4. Cross-request prefix caching is not the normal decode cache

Every running autoregressive request keeps private KV state so its next token can attend to its own earlier tokens. That cache grows as the request decodes and is not, by itself, a cross-request optimization.

Prefix caching stores read-only KV blocks produced during prefill, then lets a later independent request reuse a longest exact token-prefix match. For example, Request A and Request B may both contain the same system prompt and long document but ask different final questions. A cache hit skips prefill for the shared tokens; each request still computes its unique suffix and its own generated tokens. Therefore prefix caching improves prefill work and often TTFT, but does not make a long independent decode faster.

The cache key must include the ordered token prefix plus all execution-relevant identity: model snapshot, tokenizer/chat template, adapter, positional configuration, and multimodal input hashes. In a multi-tenant service it also includes a trust-group salt, so one tenant cannot infer another tenant's prompt from a faster cache hit. Cache only complete memory blocks; the unmatched or partial tail is prefetched normally.

## 5. Cache-aware routing and the new trade-offs

After tokenization, a prefix-cache index returns the longest matched prefix and the replicas where its KV blocks are resident. The router prefers a healthy, model-ready replica with a local hit, then the fixed-batch scheduler fills compatible work there. A miss follows normal prefill and inserts reusable full blocks after successful execution. The cache needs reference counts for live users, bounded memory, and an eviction policy such as LRU for unpinned blocks.

This creates trade-offs that a good design must name. Always sending warm requests to one worker can improve hit rate but overload that worker and starve cold work. A remote cache hit can be worse than local prefill if transferring KV blocks costs more than recomputation. Retaining popular prefixes raises hit rate but consumes HBM and reduces active batch capacity. Cross-tenant sharing improves aggregate efficiency but is usually unacceptable without isolation. I would use cache affinity as a score, with queue-age and service-class guardrails, not as an absolute routing rule.

## 6. GPU fleet, failures, and backpressure

A GPU-aware dispatcher leases work to healthy workers that report model residency, free memory, cache pressure, executor occupancy, batch duration, and heartbeat health. Model placement is separate from request scheduling: the placement controller decides which replicas exist; the router chooses among ready replicas. Workers durably write item results before completing a lease.

Leases expire and are reclaimed after worker loss. Completion is idempotent by batch and item attempt ID, so a late worker cannot overwrite a newer retry. The service bounds durable queues and returns capacity exhaustion when it cannot safely accept more work; that is admission backpressure, not a traffic-rate policy.

## 7. What to measure and how to tune

The dashboard must split queue, prefill, decode, and result-write time. For streaming traffic, track p95/p99 TTFT, TPOT or ITL, end-to-end latency, and output-token throughput. For batch traffic, track p95/p99 completion time, cost per completed item, batch fill ratio, and throughput. In both cases track cache hit rate, cached prefill tokens, cache residency and eviction rate, GPU memory use, queue age, cancellation outcome, and errors.

Tune B, W, cache capacity, and cache-affinity weight by workload slice rather than global average. Compare warm and cold requests separately; a lower fleet-wide mean can still hide an unacceptable cold-request p99.

## 8. Review-mode critique

I would flag a design that calls every cache a KV cache without distinguishing private decode state from cross-request prefix reuse; uses only average latency; routes entirely by cache affinity; omits model and tenant identity from cache keys; or measures cache hits without measuring how much prefill time and TTFT they actually saved. I would also ask whether the service is really an offline batch API, because claiming a TTFT improvement without a streaming contract is a metric mismatch.
